name: Sodium carbonates
text:
This group covers sodium carbonate (soda ash), sodium bicarbonate (baking soda) and sodium sesquicarbonate. They are mineral salts, produced industrially or obtained from natural deposits such as the mineral trona.

In food they act as acidity regulators, anti-caking agents, raising agents and stabilisers. Baking soda releases carbon dioxide when heated or mixed with an acid, so it is used to leaven cakes, quick breads, soda bread and other baked goods, and it is a main ingredient of baking powder.

name: Potassium carbonates
text:
This group includes potassium carbonate and potassium bicarbonate (potassium hydrogen carbonate). They are mineral salts made industrially; potassium carbonate is the main component of potash, historically obtained from wood ash.

In food they work as acidity regulators and stabilisers. Potassium carbonate is used to alkalise cocoa in the production of Dutch-process cocoa powder and as a raising agent in traditional German gingerbread. Potassium bicarbonate is used in winemaking and serves as a sodium-free source of carbon dioxide for leavening, including in low-sodium baking powders.

name: Ammonium carbonates
text:
This group includes ammonium carbonate and ammonium bicarbonate (ammonium hydrogen carbonate), salts produced from ammonia and carbon dioxide. When heated they break down into ammonia, carbon dioxide and water.

In food they act as acidity regulators and raising agents. They are used in flat baked goods such as crackers and cookies and in traditional recipes from northern Europe and Scandinavia, such as speculoos and Lebkuchen.

name: Magnesium carbonates
text:
This group includes magnesium carbonate and magnesium hydroxide carbonate (basic magnesium carbonate). Magnesium carbonate occurs naturally as the mineral magnesite and can also be made by precipitation from solutions of magnesium salts.

In food they work as acidity regulators and anti-caking agents; magnesium carbonate was first added to table salt in 1911 to keep it free-flowing. Magnesium carbonate can also serve as a colour retention agent, and magnesium hydroxide carbonate as a carrier and drying agent.

name: Ferrous carbonate
text:
Ferrous carbonate, or iron(II) carbonate, is an iron salt that occurs in nature as the mineral siderite and can also be prepared from solutions of iron(II) salts and sodium carbonate or bicarbonate. Its food-additive function is acidity regulator.

It has also been used as an iron supplement to treat anaemia.

name: Hydrochloric acid
text:
Hydrochloric acid is a strong mineral acid, a solution of hydrogen chloride in water, made industrially. The same acid is the main component of human gastric acid.

Its food-additive function is acidity regulator. Food-grade hydrochloric acid is used to control the pH of process water and in chemical reactions used to produce food ingredients and additives, for example gelatine, fructose, citric acid, aspartame and hydrolysed vegetable protein.

name: Potassium chloride
text:
Potassium chloride is a mineral salt that occurs naturally as sylvite and is extracted from minerals such as sylvite and carnallite and from ancient dried lake deposits. Its solutions taste salty, but many people notice a bitter or metallic aftertaste.

It is used as a salt substitute, often mixed with ordinary table salt to make low-sodium salt. As a food additive it serves as a flavour enhancer, firming agent and as a synergist for stabilisers and thickeners.

name: Calcium chloride
text:
Calcium chloride is a mineral salt obtained by purification of natural brines or as a by-product of the Solvay process, which uses limestone.

In food it is used mainly as a firming agent, for example in canned tomatoes, pickled cucumbers and fruits such as apples, strawberries and peaches. It is also used to set tofu, to restore the calcium balance of processed milk in cheesemaking, to correct the mineral content of brewing water, and as a sequestrant. Its salty taste is used to flavour pickles without adding sodium.

name: Ammonium chloride
text:
Ammonium chloride is the salt of ammonia and hydrochloric acid, also known as sal ammoniac or salmiak.

In food it has been used as a yeast nutrient in bread making and as an acidifier; in baking it gives cookies a very crisp texture. It is also used to flavour salty liquorice sweets, popular in the Nordic countries, the Benelux and northern Germany.

name: Magnesium chloride
text:
Magnesium chloride is a mineral salt extracted from brine and sea water, for example from the Great Salt Lake and the Dead Sea. Magnesium ions taste bitter, and its solutions are bitter to varying degrees.

In food it is an important coagulant for making tofu from soy milk; in Japan it is sold as nigari, a powder obtained from sea water after the table salt has been removed. It can also act as a firming agent, colour retention agent and stabiliser, and it is used in nutritional and pharmaceutical magnesium preparations.

name: Stannous chloride
text:
Stannous chloride, or tin(II) chloride, is a tin salt made by reacting tin metal with hydrogen chloride or hydrochloric acid.

It acts as a colour retention agent and antioxidant in some canned and bottled foods. In the EU its only listed food use is in canned or bottled white asparagus.

In 2018 EFSA re-evaluated it and concluded that it is of no safety concern at its current use and use levels; absorption from the gut is low.

name: Sulphuric acid
text:
Sulphuric acid is a strong mineral acid produced industrially on a very large scale. Concentrated, it is highly corrosive and strongly dehydrating.

As a food additive its function is acidity regulator.

name: Sodium sulphates
text:
This group includes sodium sulfate and sodium hydrogen sulfate (sodium bisulfate). About two thirds of the world's sodium sulfate decahydrate (Glauber's salt) comes from the natural mineral mirabilite; the rest is a by-product of other chemical processes. Sodium bisulfate is an acid salt made from sulfuric acid; its solutions are strongly acidic.

In food both serve as acidity regulators.

name: Potassium sulphates
text:
This group includes potassium sulfate and potassium hydrogen sulfate (potassium bisulfate). Potassium sulfate is obtained mainly from natural salt minerals such as langbeinite and kainite and is widely used as a fertiliser. Potassium bisulfate is used to prepare potassium bitartrate for winemaking.

In food both serve as acidity regulators.

name: Calcium sulphate
text:
Calcium sulfate occurs naturally as the minerals gypsum and anhydrite and is also produced as a by-product of industrial processes such as flue-gas desulfurisation.

In food it is used as a coagulant for tofu and also serves as a firming agent, flour treatment agent, sequestrant, acidity regulator and stabiliser. It is used in products such as cheese, cereal flours, bakery products, frozen desserts and some sweets.

name: Ammonium sulphate
text:
Ammonium sulfate is an inorganic salt prepared by neutralising sulfuric acid with ammonia. Its main use is as a fertiliser.

In food it is used as a yeast nutrient in bread and serves as a dough strengthener, flour treatment agent, firming agent and stabiliser. Typical uses are baked goods, gelatin desserts and puddings.

name: Magnesium sulfate
text:
Magnesium sulfate occurs in nature as minerals such as epsomite and is a significant component of the water of some springs. Its heptahydrate is known as Epsom salt. It is also made by neutralising magnesium oxide, hydroxide or carbonate with sulfuric acid.

In food it serves as a firming agent and flavour enhancer and as a source of magnesium. It is used as a brewing salt in beer making, as a coagulant for tofu and to add taste to bottled water.

name: Copper(II) sulfate
text:
Copper(II) sulfate, or cupric sulfate, is a copper salt usually used as its bright blue pentahydrate. It is made by treating copper metal or copper oxides with sulfuric acid and is widely used as a fungicide in agriculture.

As a food additive it can serve as a colour retention agent and preservative, and it is also used as a nutrient supplement providing copper. Copper sulfate is toxic and was formerly used as an emetic.

name: Aluminium sulphate
text:
Aluminium sulfate is an aluminium salt prepared from bauxite or clay and sulfuric acid. Its main use is as a coagulant in the purification of drinking water and in wastewater treatment, and it is also used in paper manufacturing.

In food it is sometimes used as a firming agent. In the EU, as part of a 2012 reduction in the use of aluminium-containing additives, its food uses were narrowed from 2014 to candied cherries and liquid egg white for egg foams.

name: Aluminium sodium sulphate
text:
Aluminium sodium sulfate, also called soda alum or sodium alum, is a double salt produced by combining sodium sulfate and aluminium sulfate.

In food it serves as an acidity regulator and firming agent. In the US some brands of double-acting baking powder combine it with sodium bicarbonate and monocalcium phosphate.

name: Aluminium potassium sulphate
text:
Aluminium potassium sulfate, known as potash alum, is a double sulfate salt that occurs in nature as minerals and is also produced from alunite. Since antiquity it has been used as a mordant in dyeing, and it is also used in water purification and tanning.

In food it acts as an acidity regulator and stabiliser. Its chief culinary use is in pickling, to add crispness to fruit and vegetables.

name: Aluminium ammonium sulphate
text:
Aluminium ammonium sulfate, or ammonium alum, is a double sulfate of aluminium and ammonium, made from aluminium hydroxide, sulfuric acid and ammonium sulfate. It occurs naturally as the rare mineral tschermigite and is also used in water purification, tanning and dyeing.

In food it can serve as an acidity regulator, colour retention agent, firming agent, raising agent and stabiliser.

name: Sodium hydroxide
text:
Sodium hydroxide, also called caustic soda or lye, is a strong alkali produced industrially by electrolysis of salt solution (the chloralkali process). In concentrated form it is corrosive.

In food it is used as an acidity regulator and processing aid. Uses include chemical peeling of fruit and vegetables, cocoa and chocolate processing, caramel colour production and softening olives. Pretzels and German lye rolls are dipped in it before baking to give their crust, and it is used for Chinese yellow noodles, century eggs and Norwegian lutefisk.

name: Potassium hydroxide
text:
Potassium hydroxide, known as caustic potash, is a strong alkali produced industrially by electrolysis of potassium chloride solution. In concentrated form it is corrosive.

In food it is used as an acidity regulator. Food-grade potassium hydroxide is used to remove bitterness from olives and in the manufacture of cocoa.

name: Calcium hydroxide
text:
Calcium hydroxide, or slaked lime, is produced by mixing quicklime (calcium oxide) with water; quicklime is made by heating limestone.

In food it works as an acidity regulator and firming agent. It is used to clarify raw juice from sugar cane and sugar beet in sugar refining, in pickling cucumbers and other foods, and in nixtamalisation, in which maize is cooked with lime to make hominy. It is also used as a calcium supplement in fruit drinks and infant formula.

name: Ammonium hydroxide
text:
Ammonium hydroxide is a solution of ammonia in water, produced by passing ammonia gas into water. It has a highly pungent smell.

In food it is used as an acidity regulator to lower the acidity of foods. Its pH-controlling action also makes it an effective antimicrobial agent.

name: Magnesium hydroxide
text:
Magnesium hydroxide is a white compound that occurs in nature as the mineral brucite. Industrially it is produced by treating sea water with lime. It is a common component of antacids such as milk of magnesia.

In food it is used as an acidity regulator and colour retention agent.

name: Calcium oxide
text:
Calcium oxide, or quicklime, is made by heating limestone or other calcium carbonate materials, such as seashells, in a lime kiln. It reacts with water, releasing heat, to form calcium hydroxide.

In food it is used as an acidity regulator, a flour treatment agent and a raising agent.

name: Magnesium oxide
text:
Magnesium oxide, or magnesia, is a white solid that occurs naturally as the mineral periclase. It is produced by heating magnesium carbonate or magnesium hydroxide, the latter usually obtained from sea water. It is also used as an antacid, a magnesium supplement and a short-term laxative.

In food it works as an anti-caking agent and acidity regulator. Examples of its use include cocoa products, canned peas and frozen desserts.

name: Iron tartrate
text:
Iron tartrate is a complex of iron(III) with tartrate (meso-tartrate), made from sodium tartrates and iron(III) chloride.

It is used as an anti-caking agent in salt and salt substitutes. Applied to salt as a dilute solution, it changes the surface of the crystals so that they do not form solid bridges and stick together in humid conditions.

name: Sodium ferrocyanide
text:
Sodium ferrocyanide, known as yellow prussiate of soda, is a yellow crystalline salt produced industrially from hydrogen cyanide, iron(II) chloride and calcium hydroxide.

It is used as an anti-caking agent in table salt and salt substitutes.

Despite its cyanide groups it has low toxicity: little is absorbed and it does not accumulate in the body. The kidney is the target organ in animal studies. In 2018 EFSA set a group acceptable daily intake for sodium, potassium and calcium ferrocyanide of 0.03 mg/kg body weight, expressed as ferrocyanide ion, and found no safety concern at the levels used.

name: Potassium ferrocyanide
text:
Potassium ferrocyanide, known as yellow prussiate of potash, forms lemon-yellow crystals. It is produced industrially from hydrogen cyanide, iron(II) chloride and calcium hydroxide.

It is used as an anti-caking agent in table salt and salt substitutes, and it is also used in wine production.

Despite its cyanide groups it has low toxicity: little is absorbed and it does not accumulate in the body. The kidney is the target organ in animal studies. In 2018 EFSA set a group acceptable daily intake for sodium, potassium and calcium ferrocyanide of 0.03 mg/kg body weight, expressed as ferrocyanide ion, and found no safety concern at the levels used.

name: Ferrous hexacyanomanganate
text: Ferrous hexacyanomanganate is a complex cyanide compound of iron and manganese. It has been assigned the function of an anti-caking agent.

name: Calcium ferrocyanide
text:
Calcium ferrocyanide is the calcium salt of the ferrocyanide complex ion, a yellow solid that is insoluble in water. It is used as a precursor of the pigment Prussian blue.

In food it is used as an anti-caking agent in table salt and salt substitutes.

Despite its cyanide groups it has low toxicity: little is absorbed and it does not accumulate in the body. The kidney is the target organ in animal studies. In 2018 EFSA set a group acceptable daily intake for sodium, potassium and calcium ferrocyanide of 0.03 mg/kg body weight, expressed as ferrocyanide ion, and found no safety concern at the levels used.

name: Sodium thiosulfate
text:
Sodium thiosulfate, historically called hyposulphite of soda, is an inorganic salt prepared synthetically from sulfur compounds. Outside food it is used as a photographic fixer, to dechlorinate water and as a medical treatment for cyanide poisoning.

In food it acts as an antioxidant (preventing browning), sequestrant and reducing agent. Typical uses are table salt and alcoholic beverages.

name: Dicalcium diphosphate
text:
The number 540 was the serial number of dicalcium diphosphate (calcium pyrophosphate) in British food labelling rules of the 1980s, a national number without the E prefix. The current international numbering system no longer uses 540 and lists dicalcium diphosphate with the other diphosphates as 450(vi).

Dicalcium diphosphate is a fine, white, odourless powder that is insoluble in water. In food it serves as a buffering and neutralising agent and as a yeast food. JECFA includes it in a group maximum tolerable daily intake of 70 mg/kg body weight for phosphorus from all food sources.

name: Sodium aluminium phosphate, acidic
text:
Sodium aluminium phosphates are inorganic salts made by combining alumina, phosphoric acid and sodium hydroxide. They exist in acidic and basic forms.

The acidic form is used as the acid component of baking powders for leavening baked goods. It reacts with baking soda to release carbon dioxide, mostly at baking temperatures rather than during mixing, and has a neutral flavour. Its other functions include acidity regulator, emulsifier and stabiliser. Basic forms are used in cheese making.

Because of concern about aluminium intake, in 2012 the EU restricted its use, from 2014, to sponge cakes made of contrasting coloured segments, such as Battenberg cake.

name: Bone phosphate
text:
Bone phosphate is a calcium phosphate made from animal bones, so it is of animal origin.

Its technological functions in food include anti-caking agent, emulsifier, humectant, stabiliser and thickener.

name: Calcium sodium polyphosphate
text:
Calcium sodium polyphosphate is a polyphosphate salt containing calcium and sodium. In the current international numbering system it is listed with the other polyphosphates as 452(iii); the number 543 is no longer used there.

In food, polyphosphates of this kind can act as acidity regulators, emulsifiers, humectants, raising agents, sequestrants and stabilisers.

name: Calcium polyphosphate
text:
Calcium polyphosphate is a polyphosphate salt of calcium. The number 544 was its serial number in British food labelling rules of the 1980s; the current international numbering system lists it with the other polyphosphates as 452(iv).

In food it can act as an acidity regulator, emulsifier, emulsifying salt, humectant, raising agent, sequestrant, stabiliser and thickener.

name: Ammonium polyphosphate
text:
Ammonium polyphosphate is an inorganic salt of polyphosphoric acid and ammonia, with chain-like and sometimes branched molecules. Outside food it is used as a fertiliser and as a flame retardant in paints, coatings and plastics.

In food it acts as an emulsifier; its other technological functions include acidity regulator, humectant, sequestrant, stabiliser and thickener.

name: Sodium silicates
text:
This group covers sodium silicate (water glass) and sodium metasilicate. Sodium silicates can be made by dissolving silica in molten sodium carbonate, and most of them dissolve in water to give alkaline solutions.

In food they are classed as anti-caking agents. Their main uses are outside food: detergents, paper making, water treatment, construction materials and adhesives. Historically, water glass solution was used to preserve fresh eggs by sealing the shell.

name: Silicon dioxide
text:
Silicon dioxide, or silica, is a compound of silicon and oxygen found in nature as quartz and as the main constituent of sand. The forms used as a food additive are synthetic amorphous silicas, such as fumed and precipitated silica.

It is used mainly as a flow or anti-caking agent in powdered foods such as spices and non-dairy coffee creamer, and in powders pressed into tablets. It can absorb water. Colloidal silica is also used to clarify wine, beer and juice.

In 2024 EFSA concluded that it does not raise a safety concern at the reported uses and use levels, including in food for infants under 16 weeks.

name: Calcium silicate
text:
Calcium silicate is a compound of calcium oxide and silica; it occurs naturally as the mineral larnite. It is a white, free-flowing powder, and is also widely used in high-temperature insulation materials.

In food it is used as an anti-caking agent, for example in table salt.

In 2018 EFSA found its absorption to be very low but concluded that its safety as a food additive could not be assessed, because reliable long-term toxicity data were lacking.

name: Magnesium silicates
text:
This group covers synthetic magnesium silicate and magnesium trisilicate, compounds of magnesium and silica.

In food they serve as anti-caking and dusting agents. Magnesium trisilicate is also used to treat frying oil, where it absorbs fatty acids and other impurities, and is used in medicine as an antacid.

In 2018 EFSA found their absorption to be very low but concluded that their safety as food additives could not be assessed, because reliable long-term toxicity data were lacking.

name: Talc
text:
Talc is a natural clay mineral composed of hydrated magnesium silicate. It is widely used in plastics, paper, paints, ceramics and cosmetics.

In food it acts as an anti-caking and dusting agent and as a glazing agent, and it may be used to polish white rice. It is also used in tablets to help powders flow. The EU specification for food-grade talc requires it to be free of asbestos.

In 2018 EFSA found its absorption to be very low but concluded that its safety as a food additive could not be assessed, because reliable long-term toxicity data were lacking.

name: Sodium aluminium silicate
text:
Sodium aluminium silicate, or sodium aluminosilicate, is a compound of sodium, aluminium, silicon and oxygen, which may also contain water. The food additive is a synthetic amorphous form produced with a range of compositions; related compounds include natural minerals and synthetic zeolites.

In food it acts as an anti-caking (free-flow) agent.

In 2020 EFSA concluded that its safety could not be assessed because of very limited data, and calculated that aluminium intake from its reported use in food supplements would exceed the tolerable weekly intake for aluminium.

name: Potassium aluminium silicate
text:
Potassium aluminium silicate as a food additive is mica: natural mica consisting mainly of the mineral muscovite, in the form of light grey to white platelets or powder.

In food it is classed as an anti-caking agent and a carrier. In practice it is used as an inseparable component of pearlescent pigments, as a carrier for the colours titanium dioxide (E171) and iron oxides (E172).

In 2020 EFSA concluded that its safety could not be assessed because toxicological data and characterisation were insufficient, and noted that aluminium intake from its use as a colour carrier at the maximum level could theoretically far exceed the tolerable weekly intake.

name: Calcium aluminium silicate
text:
Calcium aluminium silicate, or calcium aluminosilicate, is a compound containing calcium, aluminium and silica, most commonly CaAl2Si2O8. In nature it occurs as the feldspar mineral anorthite.

In food it has been used as an anti-caking agent.

In 2012 the EU decided to remove it from its list of food additives, with authorisation ending on 31 January 2014. This was part of a reduction in aluminium-containing additives after the tolerable weekly intake for aluminium was lowered; the substance was considered replaceable by other additives.

name: Zinc silicate
text:
Zinc silicate is a compound of zinc and silica; naturally occurring zinc silicates include the minerals willemite and hemimorphite.

As a food additive it is classed as an anti-caking agent.

name: Bentonite
text:
Bentonite is an absorbent swelling clay made up mostly of montmorillonite. It usually forms from the weathering of volcanic ash and can absorb large amounts of water.

As a food additive it is classed as an anti-caking agent and was used as a carrier. Bentonite is also used to decolourise oils and to clarify wine, cider, beer, mead and vinegar; in winemaking it removes excess protein from white wines.

In 2012 the EU removed this aluminium-containing substance from its list of food additives, with authorisation ending on 31 May 2013, because manufacturers no longer used it as a carrier.

name: Aluminium silicate (kaolin)
text:
Aluminium silicate in this sense is kaolin, or china clay: a soft, usually white clay rich in the mineral kaolinite, a layered aluminium silicate. Kaolin is used mainly in paper and ceramics, and also in paints, toothpaste and medicines for diarrhoea.

As a food additive it is classed as an anti-caking agent.

In 2012 the EU decided to remove it from its list of food additives, with authorisation ending on 31 January 2014. This was part of a reduction in aluminium-containing additives after the tolerable weekly intake for aluminium was lowered; kaolin was considered replaceable by other additives.

name: Potassium silicate
text:
Potassium silicate is the name for a family of inorganic compounds, most commonly K2SiO3; it can be made by treating silica with potassium hydroxide. Its solutions are strongly alkaline.

As a food additive it is classed as an anti-caking agent. Its other uses include fire-proofing wood, horticulture as a source of potassium and silica, metal cleaners and welding rods.

name: Vermiculite
text:
Vermiculite is a natural hydrous silicate mineral of magnesium, aluminium and iron that expands strongly when heated. Expanded vermiculite is used in insulation, lightweight concrete and fireproof wallboard, and in growing media for plants.

Its E number belongs to animal feed rather than food: it is used as a binder and anti-caking agent in feed. In 2020 EFSA considered it safe for consumers and the environment under the proposed conditions of use in feed.

name: Sepiolite
text:
Sepiolite, also called meerschaum, is a soft white clay mineral, a complex hydrated magnesium silicate that is sometimes fibrous. It is used as an absorbent and to make tobacco pipes.

It is used in animal feed as a binder, anti-caking agent and thickener. In 2022 EFSA concluded that its use in feed is safe for consumers, but that the dusty additive is a respiratory irritant for people handling it.

name: Sepiolitic clay
text:
Sepiolitic clay is a natural clay containing the mineral sepiolite, a hydrated magnesium silicate.

It is used in animal feed as a binder and anti-caking agent. In 2022 EFSA concluded that it is unlikely to be absorbed and that its use in feed is safe for consumers.

name: Lignosulfonates
text:
Lignosulfonates are water-soluble polymers derived from lignin, the natural binding material of wood. They are by-products of making wood pulp by the sulfite process, and are used as dispersants and binders, for example in particle board, road dust control and water treatment. Oxidising softwood lignosulfonates was a route to vanillin, the artificial vanilla flavour.

In animal feed they are used as pellet binders. In 2015 EFSA found no concern for consumer safety from their use in animal nutrition.

name: Natrolite-phonolite
text:
Natrolite-phonolite is a ground volcanic rock: phonolite, an uncommon igneous rock, here containing natrolite, a zeolite mineral made of hydrated sodium aluminium silicate.

It is used as an anti-caking agent in animal feed. In 2023 EFSA found no indication of substantial absorption and therefore no concern for consumers, but could not conclude on its safety for the animals or on its efficacy because of insufficient data.

name: Fatty acids
text:
Fatty acids are the carboxylic acids that make up fats and oils; industrially they are usually produced by splitting (hydrolysing) fats and oils. The food additive covers caprylic, capric, lauric, myristic, palmitic, stearic and oleic acid, alone or in combination.

In food they act as antifoaming agents, glazing agents and foam stabilisers.

In 2017 EFSA noted that they are absorbed in the same way as fatty acids from the normal diet and concluded that they are of no safety concern at the reported uses and use levels.

name: Magnesium stearate
text:
Magnesium stearate is the magnesium salt of stearic acid, a white, water-insoluble powder. It is made by reacting sodium stearate with magnesium salts or by treating magnesium oxide with stearic acid.

It is the most widely used lubricant in making tablets and capsules, where it stops powders sticking to equipment. In food it is used as an anti-adherent and anti-caking agent.

The number 572 was its serial number in British food labelling rules of the 1980s. In the EU numbering it falls under E470b, magnesium salts of fatty acids.

name: Gluconic acid
text:
Gluconic acid is an organic acid formed by oxidation of glucose, typically with the enzyme glucose oxidase or by fermentation, for example with the mould Aspergillus niger. It occurs naturally in fruit, honey and wine.

In food it is used as an acidity regulator and raising agent.

name: Glucono-delta-lactone
text:
Glucono-delta-lactone (GDL), also called gluconolactone, is a lactone of gluconic acid. It is typically made by oxidising glucose with the enzyme glucose oxidase and is a white, odourless crystalline powder.

GDL itself is pH-neutral, but in water it slowly turns into gluconic acid, which adds a tangy taste with about a third of the sourness of citric acid. It is used as an acidifier, sequestrant, raising agent and curing or pickling agent, and has been marketed for use in feta cheese. The body metabolises it, yielding about as much energy per gram as sugar.

name: Sodium gluconate
text:
Sodium gluconate is the sodium salt of gluconic acid, a white, water-soluble powder. Commercially, glucose is fermented by microorganisms such as Aspergillus niger to gluconic acid, which is then neutralised with sodium hydroxide.

In food it is used mainly as a sequestrant, binding metal ions that could affect colour, flavour or stability; it can also act as a stabiliser and thickener. Outside food it is used as a chelating agent in cleaning products, textile dyeing and metal surface treatment.

name: Potassium gluconate
text:
Potassium gluconate is the potassium salt of gluconic acid. It is also sold as a mineral supplement providing potassium.

In food it is used as an acidity regulator and sequestrant, binding metal ions, and as a yeast food.

name: Calcium gluconate
text:
Calcium gluconate is the calcium salt of gluconic acid. It is produced commercially by oxidising glucose chemically or electrolytically, or by fermentation. It is used as a calcium supplement and as a medicine, for example given into a vein to treat low blood calcium, and as a gel for hydrofluoric acid burns.

In food it acts as an acidity regulator, firming agent and sequestrant.

name: Ferrous gluconate
text:
Ferrous gluconate, or iron(II) gluconate, is the iron(II) salt of gluconic acid, a black compound often used as an iron supplement.

In food it is a colour retention agent, used mainly in processing black olives, to which it gives a uniform jet-black colour.

In overdose it can be toxic, particularly to children.

name: Magnesium gluconate
text:
Magnesium gluconate is the magnesium salt of gluconic acid. It has been studied as a source of magnesium in supplements.

In food it can act as an acidity regulator, firming agent and flavour enhancer.

name: Ferrous lactate
text:
Ferrous lactate, or iron(II) lactate, is a compound of iron(II) with lactic acid. It can be made, for example, from calcium lactate and iron(II) sulfate. It is also used as a remedy for iron deficiency.

In food it is a colour retention agent, used for example for olives, and it can also act as an acidity regulator.

name: 4-Hexylresorcinol
text:
4-Hexylresorcinol is an organic compound with antiseptic and local anaesthetic properties. It is used in throat lozenges and topical antiseptics, and in skin-care products.

In food it acts as an antioxidant and colour retention agent. It is used on shrimp and other crustaceans to reduce melanosis, the formation of black spots, which extends shelf life.

name: Synthetic calcium aluminates
text:
Calcium aluminates are materials obtained by heating calcium oxide and aluminium oxide together at high temperatures. They are used mainly in refractories and cements.

The number E598 comes from European rules on additives for animal feed. There a synthetic mixture of calcium aluminates containing 35 to 51% aluminium oxide was listed as a binder and anti-caking agent in feed for poultry, rabbits, pigs, cattle, lambs and kids; that feed listing was withdrawn in 2017.

name: Perlite
text:
Perlite is a natural volcanic glass with a relatively high water content. When heated it expands to 7 to 16 times its volume, forming a light, white, porous material. It is used as a filter aid, for example for beer, in horticulture, and in cosmetics as an absorbent and exfoliant.

In animal feed it is used as an anti-caking agent. In 2025 EFSA concluded that this use is safe for consumers and the environment.
